/Issued 1207 AM MDT Fri Oct 9 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

The next incoming trough coming down from Canada will bring an 
increase in winds aloft today. These stronger winds aloft will 
mix down to the surface from day time vertical mixing. The 
combination of the warm, breezy, and dry conditons will bring 
elevated to critical fire weather conditions to the region. 
Temperatures are also expected to peak today, with numerous lower 
elevation locations reaching into the 80s. 

Saturday, an elongated trough coming in from Canada will bring a 
multi-day weather system through Montana. A cold front passing 
from north to south Saturday morning bring the first rush of 
cooler air to the region along with mountain snow and lower 
elevation rain/snow. Lee troughing with northerly cold air 
advection continues behind the front, and transitions rain to snow
at lower elevations by Saturday evening. Meanwhile the front 
progression slows down heading into Southwest MT, which delays the
switch over the snow later than North-Central MT. Strong 
convergence and frontogenesis also occurs along this front as it
head into North-Central/Central MT, which can develop moderate to
heavy snow banding. Northerly flow in North-Central MT will allow
for enhanced snowfall for northerly upslope areas of the Little 
Belts/Central Continental Divide. Temperatures don't look to warm
up much heading into Sunday. Increasing moisture from the 
remnant southwest tropical storm system will continue to feed 
moisture into this storm system Sunday into Monday before exiting 
later in the day Monday.

Behind this system, another quick moving trough looks to swing 
through Wednesday into Thursday, which will keep the cooler 
temperatures and chances of precipitation. However, details with 
this will be heavily dependent on what happens this 
weekend/Monday. 

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Even though we are closer in time to this next weather system, there 
remains some uncertainty in the progression of this system. This 
is due to the remnant of the tropical system Rachel lifting north
from the Southwest U.S. and into the Rockies. The first 
uncertainty is the cold front timing Saturday. Some recent trends
slow down the front progression later into the afternoon Saturday
across North-Central MT which will bring a slower transition to 
rain to snow. Some solutions have this earlier cold front timing 
Saturday morning, which bring a quicker transition to rain to 
snow as temperatures will struggle to heat up with diurnal 
daytime heating. Another factor is if any moderate to heavy snow 
banding can dynamically cool the atmosphere quicker, leading to a
quicker rain to snow transition.

The second uncertainty is where the better convergence and 
frontogenesis enhanced snow banding sets up. Models were trending 
towards Central/North-Central MT, but some recent runs have that 
cold front and surface low stalling by the MT and ID border. As a 
result, there also could be moderate to heavy snowfall in 
Southwest MT Sunday into Monday. For Central/North-Central MT,
any moderate to heavier snow banding can crash surface/road
temperatures, leading to quicker accumulations. Probabilities for
6" of snow along the Montana Highway 200 corridor and northerly
upslope areas of Cascade and Judith Basin Counties run 50%
chances. However, the concerns of these snow bands developing gave
the nudges to expand the Winter Storm Watches into those areas 
and the Meagher County Valley. That front stalling out near the 
MT/ID border combined with the warm, moist tropical airmass 
overriding the boundary may also bring concerns for a wintry mix 
along the state border.

The main impacts from this weather system will be wet snow 
weighing down power lines and trees, leading to power outages and 
damaged trees. Temperatures dropping into the 20s Sunday morning 
will allow for wet pavements to freeze and become slippery. Colder
temperatures will also impact any outdoor recreation in the 
mountains/back country and travel over mountain passes will be 
impacted by heavy, wet snow. -Wilson
